question: What minimum RBC ratio does one of LLANY's reinsurance arrangements require, and how does that compare with the RBC range that triggers the regulator's company action level?

answer.text:
One of LLANY's reinsurance arrangements requires it to maintain an RBC ratio of at least 185% or an S&P capital adequacy ratio of 115% [5]. (Its largest indemnity reinsurance arrangement has a lower minimum, an RBC ratio of at least 160% or an S&P capital adequacy ratio of 100% [5].)

The "company action level" is triggered when the RBC ratio is between 75% and 100%. At that point the insurer must submit a plan to the regulator describing the corrective action it proposes [3][4].

Comparison: the 185% contractual minimum is 85 percentage points above the top of the 75%–100% company action level band. The 160% minimum on the largest arrangement is 60 points above that band. So LLANY must stay well above the regulatory trigger zone to avoid the cedent recapturing the business [5].

question: Why does Principal Financial Group's capacity to return capital hinge on Principal Life, and how much could Principal Life pay out in 2026 without asking the Iowa regulator?

answer.text:
Why it hinges on Principal Life: Principal Financial Group (PFG) is an insurance holding company whose assets include all the outstanding common stock of Principal Life and other subsidiaries. Its ability to pay stockholder dividends, repurchase shares, and meet obligations (operating expenses and debt service) depends on dividends or other distributions it receives from Principal Life. Iowa insurance laws limit what Principal Life can pay to its parent, so any inability of Principal Life to pay could leave PFG unable to pay dividends to stockholders or meet other obligations [2].

The Iowa limits: Principal Life may pay dividends only from earned surplus arising from its business. It needs prior approval from the Iowa Commissioner of Insurance if a distribution would exceed certain statutory limits, and the Commissioner has discretion to disapprove requests above those limits [1][3]. Extraordinary dividends are those that, together with other distributions in the preceding twelve months, exceed the greater of (i) 10% of statutory policyholder surplus at the prior year-end (excluding admitted disallowed interest maintenance reserve) or (ii) the prior calendar year's statutory net gain from operations, not to exceed earned surplus [1][3].

2026 capacity: Based on 2025 statutory results, Principal Life could pay approximately $1,234.0 million in ordinary stockholder dividends in 2026 without prior regulatory approval [3][1]. One caveat: because the test looks at dividends paid over rolling twelve-month periods, dividends paid before a specified date in 2026 could be partly or wholly extraordinary and need approval [5].

Context: Principal Life paid $1,055.0 million in dividends to its parent in 2025 and $1,010.0 million in 2024, all of it extraordinary and approved by the Commissioner [5]. PFG also had $2,362.3 million of cash and liquid assets in its holding companies and other subsidiaries at December 31, 2025, available for corporate purposes [5].
